title: Ray White Retires … After a Quick 44.5 Years
content:
Let’s check in with 1982.

“E.T.” landed in theaters and called home. Something called “emoticons” were posted by a computer scientist and so began the creation story of emojis. CDs appeared in record stores. And the Library’s Music Division hired Raymond White, a fresh-faced young man from University of Maryland with degrees in history and vocal performance, to a permanent position.

And lo, for all the days in the world since then until the one at the very end of this month, Ray White has been a fixture at the Library of Congress. He retires at the close of business on Friday, July 31, a mere 44.5 years after he officially started. We are sorry he is leaving so soon but will wish him the best anyhow.

Ray has delighted patrons, scholars and guests of the Library with his knowledge of the field, encompassing everything from Beethoven to Broadway show tunes, including delightful asides and bon mots about great pieces of art or how simple little songs became big hits. Though he does much work behind the scenes, he is best known for his storytelling in presenting items for guests, be they students or VIPs, to marvel over.
creator: Neely Tucker
sourceDescription: Stories from the Library of Congress

title: Two Thousand Years of “The Odyssey” at the Library
content:
Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of “The Odyssey” introduces the epic poem attributed to Homer to a new generation of moviegoers, turning a nearly 3,000-year-old story into a fresh cultural touchstone.

The Library’s vast collections, covering centuries of time, document how artists, cartographers and translators around the world have translated and reimagined Odysseus’ journey anew. From medieval engravings to graphic novels, the Library’s holdings document how each generation seems to find fresh meaning in the mythical, decade-long struggle of the Greek hero to return home to his wife, Penelope, and son, Telemachus, following the Trojan War.

The 12,000-line prose poem originated in an oral tradition more than 2,800 years ago in ancient Greece and was performed at festivals for hundreds of years. It uses monsters, murder, war, gods and disasters to pose timeless questions about loyalty and perseverance, resilience, temptation, loss and, above all, the universal search for belonging.

The Library’s holdings on work attributed to Homer go back about 2,000 years, with a papyrus fragment from “The Iliad,” the precursor to “The Odyssey,” and then continue as the centuries go by.

title: The Tombstone Edition that Helped Galvanize American Independence
content:
It’s known as the Tombstone Edition, a lightning-strike newspaper image that presages the American Revolution — and 261 years after it electrified readers in Colonial-era Philadelphia, a rare, fragile copy now rests at the Library.

Pennsylvania Journal editor and printer William Bradford, livid at Britain’s imposition of the Stamp Act on the Colonies, laid out the front page of his Oct. 31, 1765, newspaper as if it were the paper’s grave marker, complete with a skull and crossbones set at the top in heavy black type. His furious editorial said the Stamp Act’s tax on paper, a rare and expensive commodity, would kill his newspaper, others like it and therefore choke off a free press.

“EXPIRING,” read the headline, describing the paper’s fate.

“The Liberty of the Press has been very justly one of the main Pillars of the Liberty of the People,” read the front-page editorial, blasting the act as “insupportable Slavery.”

title: “Four Score and Seven Years Ago….” Lincoln’s Handwritten Gettysburg Address
content:
Lincoln’s “few appropriate remarks” would later become famous as the Gettysburg Address and continue to resonate with people around the world.

For a document as iconic as the Gettysburg Address now is, many details about its creation and delivery have been lost to time or clouded by conflicting memories of witnesses. Lincoln began working on the address in Washington, drafting his opening lines in ink on Executive Mansion stationery.

Harkening back to the Declaration of Independence 87 years earlier (“four score and seven years ago”), Lincoln noted that the Revolutionary generation had founded a new nation “conceived in liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that ‘all men are created equal.’” That nation was now being torn apart by civil war, Lincoln continued, and the question of “whether that nation, or any nation so conceived, and so dedicated, can long endure” remained to be answered. But at that ceremony, they gathered to dedicate a burial ground honoring those who gave their lives so that the nation would survive.

title: “By the Dawn’s Early Light…”
content:
—This is a guest post by Loras Schissel, a senior music specialist in the Music Division. It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

It was September 1814, and British warships were unleashing a fierce bombardment on Fort McHenry, the American fortress guarding Baltimore Harbor. Rockets streaked across the night sky, shells burst in flashes of light, the city’s fate hung in the balance.

A few miles away, Francis Scott Key watched anxiously from a British ship, where he had gone to secure the release of a captured friend. Key feared the fort had fallen — until, by dawn’s light, he saw a large American flag still waving over McHenry’s ramparts.

Inspired, Key composed a poem, “Defence of Fort M‘Henry,” about what he’d witnessed — with the tune of an 18th-century British song, “Anacreon in Heaven,” in mind for it. Key’s creation, when set to that music, forever after would be known by another name: “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Though popular from its inception, it was not officially recognized as the national anthem for another 117 years, when President Herbert Hoover signed it into law on March 3, 1931.

title: America’s Time Capsule … for 2276
content:
-This is a guest post by Brett Zongker and Deb Fiscella, both of the public affairs section in the Office of Communications. It also appears in slightly different form in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

The nation’s oldest federal cultural institution is using some of the newest technology to preserve digital copies of historical collection items for the next 250 years.

As part of America’s 250th anniversary celebrations, the Library made a trailblazing contribution to America’s Time Capsule : a tiny metal pellet holding synthetic DNA encoded with digital copies of items from the Library’s collections. The capsule itself – a 900-pound stainless steel cylinder covered by a 1,100-pound stainless steel bell jar  – was ceremonially buried 10 feet underground on July 4th at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia.

title: Napoleon, Henry VIII, Beethoven, Poe: The Amazing Autograph Collection of John D. Batchelder
content:
In 1707, the correspondent began his letter with an elaborate salutation in French: “Monsieur Mon Cousin,” he wrote, then explaining to the recipient, in effusive and flattering terms, that a small gift was en route.

He ended the note with a simple signature in his native Cyrillic script: “Peter.”

As in Peter I, Peter the Great, Peter the Tsar, Peter the Emperor, the polymath genius who by military and diplomatic turns, both brilliant and cruel, all but founded modern Russia. His hand, his attention, his touch all right there in a few strokes of a pen nib. He’s not the great man of history here; just Peter, signing off. You can almost hear the scratch of the pen across the parchment.

Three centuries later, this talisman from another time rests on a table in the Manuscript Division reading room, a stunning autograph in the John Davis Batchelder Collection, a litany of more than 1,800 signatures from bold-faced names who helped define Western politics, painting, philosophy, science, music and culture from the Renaissance to the mid-20th century.

title: Ann Patchett, Martin Scorsese, Cynthia Erivo: The 2026 National Book Festival
content:
-This is a guest post by Deb Fiscella, a public affairs specialist in the Office of Communications. 

You can watch director Martin Scorsese screen some of his favorite film clips, listen to “Wicked” star Cynthia Erivo talk about being just too much for some people and get a kick out of Ann Patchett chatting about her new bestselling book at the Library’s National Book Festival this year, coming to the Washington Convention Center on Saturday, Aug. 22.

Literary and multimedia stars such as Patrick Radden Keefe, Kate McKinnon, Tia Williams, Tayari Jones, Frank Miller and Karin Slaughter are also among more than 80 authors who will fill out the day. The festival, an annual tradition since 2001, this year is part of the Library’s series of programs, America 250: It’s Your Story, to observe the nation’s 250th birthday.

An important heads-up: Free tickets will be required for festival entry (this is a first), but not for individual programs. Tickets can be reserved at loc.gov/bookfest.

creator: Neely Tucker

title: A250: The Declaration’s Promise
content:
-This is a guest post by Ryan Reft, a historian in the Manuscript Division. It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Following the trauma of the American Civil War, Walt Whitman published “Democratic Vistas,” a tough but ultimately optimistic appraisal of America’s democratic promise. In it, Whitman reminisced about the nation’s founding and the echoes of the past from his youth: “The old men, I remember as a boy, were always talking of American independence. What is independence?”

Throughout the work, Whitman explores this question as well as the social and political fissures that needed to be traversed after the war. Amidst that wreckage, Whitman held firm to his belief in the United States’ adherence to a democratic ideal and to the principles of the Declaration of Independence.

title: Remembering Victor Willis: How He Wrote the Disco Anthem “Y.M.C.A.”
content:
–Victor Willis, the lead vocalist and primary songwriter for the Village People, died yesterday at the age of 74, his wife announced in a statement this morning. The Library inducted “Y.M.C.A.” into the National Recording Registry in 2020 and I caught up with him for a delightful phone interview. He politely recounted, in detail, how he had written one of the most iconic songs in American pop music history. We reprint it below in honor of his passing. 

Victor Willis, Mr. “Y.M.C.A.” himself, has just come upstairs from his home gym in San Diego and grabbed the telephone. Couple miles on the treadmill, pushups, weights. He’s 68, the founder and lead songwriter of the Village People and, until the coronavirus shutdowns, had 50 or 60 shows lined up this year.

“We were booked all through the year, all over the world,” Willis says.

The voice coming down the line is energetic, upbeat. Despite the postponed gigs, he’s in a good place after decades of turmoil. He’s happily married, wealthy and won a landmark copyright case a few years ago to obtain 50% royalties on the Village People hits that he co-wrote, which is all of them. He also regained control of the group’s name and performing rights.
